# Abstract

Goal-directed remembering can be less affected by interference even as the same material becomes less likely to come to mind inadvertently.
The trauma-film paradigm examines this asymmetry in memory for distressing films: a visuospatial intervention task performed after a film reminder can reduce later intrusions while leaving voluntary memory relatively intact.
This selective interference effect is often interpreted through theories of traumatic memory in which intrusive and deliberate remembering depend on differently vulnerable memory representations.
Here we show that the same dissociation may follow from retrieved-context dynamics developed to explain episodic memory more generally.
We develop this account in an emotional Context Maintenance and Retrieval (eCMR) model that predicts sequences of film and non-film recall events.
The model links task items to film-associated context reinstated by a film reminder. 
That context can later cue task competitors as well as film items.
Unguided film recall declines when reminder-linked learning makes task items strong competitors.
Deliberate recall is less affected when a maintained film-category cue favors film candidates without equally supporting task competitors.
Recognition is less affected than recall because the model evaluates a presented candidate item's fit to context rather than selecting among film and task candidates.
This account clarifies when intrusive and voluntary remembering can diverge and situates selective interference within a broader computational theory of episodic learning and retrieval.

# Introduction

Traumatic experience foregrounds a tension between accessibility and selectivity in episodic memory.
From a functional perspective, events with lasting significance need to remain accessible in memory so remembered details can guide later decisions [@zhou2025episodic].
At the same time, adaptive retrieval is selective: what comes to mind should normally depend on current goals, cues, and circumstances.
Intrusive memories after trauma show how highly accessible event memories can strain the selectivity of retrieval.
In PTSD, such memories can come to mind unbidden and poorly matched to the present, causing distress and interfering with ongoing activity [@ehlers2000cognitive; @brewin2010intrusive; @krans2009intrusive; @iyadurai2019intrusive].
Explaining how episodic memory keeps consequential event memories accessible while regulating their retrieval is therefore a shared target for both clinical science and mechanistic theories of memory.

The trauma-film paradigm provides a controlled setting for comparing intrusive and voluntary memory for the same event [@holmes2008inducing; @james2016trauma].
Participants view distressing film material, record later intrusive memories of the film, and often complete voluntary-memory tests for the same material.
This design makes it possible to ask whether the same encoded event can remain accessible to deliberate retrieval while becoming more or less likely to come to mind involuntarily.
In such research, intrusion frequency is often only weakly related to voluntary-memory performance, such that the two measures dissociate [@holmes2004trauma; @james2016trauma].
The same encoded episode can therefore support both involuntary and deliberate remembering, and these modes can come apart empirically.

Visuospatial interference tasks make this dissociation experimentally sharper.
In immediate post-film studies, tasks such as Tetris can reduce later film intrusions while voluntary memory for the same material remains relatively intact [@holmes2009can; @holmes2010key; @deeprose2012imagery; @lau2019intrusive].
Delayed variants pair the interference task with a film reminder.
Participants return after roughly 24 hours to 3 days, view reminder cues for the film, and then complete Tetris.
This reminder-plus-Tetris sequence can reduce subsequent intrusions [@james2015computer; @kessler2020visuospatial].
The resulting pattern of reduced intrusions with relatively preserved deliberate memory is termed selective interference.
@fig-empirical-target defines the qualitative pattern targeted by the recall simulations: following a film reminder, the visuospatial task has a larger effect on unguided than deliberate film recall.

Dual-representation accounts provide the prevailing theoretical interpretation of selective interference in the trauma-film literature [@brewin1996dual; @brewin2010intrusive; @brewin2014episodic].
The revised account distinguishes flexible, contextualized representations (C-reps) from inflexible, sensory-bound representations (S-reps).
C-reps bind event elements within a spatiotemporal and autobiographical context and support flexible reconstruction and top-down control, whereas S-reps preserve sensory and affective information that can be reactivated by matching situational cues [@brewin2010intrusive; @bird2012hippocampus; @bisby2020reduced].
Extreme stress is proposed to strengthen S-reps, weaken C-reps, and impair their integration, allowing sensory-bound information to be re-experienced without adequate contextualization.
C-reps may contribute to involuntary as well as voluntary access, whereas sensory-bound S-reps are proposed to have a distinctive role in involuntary re-experiencing [@brewin2010intrusive; @brewin2014episodic].

DRA's two-representation architecture gives visuospatial interference a representational interpretation.
In immediate post-film procedures, a visuospatial task is proposed to compete with sensory-perceptual imagery while film memory is being maintained and consolidated [@baddeley2000working; @holmes2009can; @holmes2010key].
In delayed procedures, a reminder is proposed to reactivate the film memory before the task, opening a period in which the memory can be modified through reconsolidation or post-reactivation updating [@kindt2009beyond; @james2015computer].
Reduced intrusions with preserved deliberate memory have accordingly been taken as support for separate traces or differently vulnerable representations, with the intervention affecting memory that supports intrusive imagery more strongly than memory that supports deliberate recollection [@deeprose2012imagery; @lau2019intrusive; @lau2021selectively].

Dual-representation theory is not silent about retrieval: its account includes situational cueing, deliberate reconstruction, and top-down control.
Its application to selective interference has nevertheless remained principally a representational explanation of why the two outcomes can differ.
No computational process model of the trauma-film selective-interference paradigm currently specifies within DRA how a reminder reinstates context, how the intervening task is learned, how film and task candidates compete, and how retrieval goals and test formats alter that competition.
The representational interpretation therefore does not by itself derive when selective interference should depend on reminder timing, task properties, deliberate-retrieval control, or whether voluntary memory is measured by recall or recognition.

Retrieved-context theory supplies established operations for explaining how reminder-linked learning creates competitors and how retrieval remains selective among them.
Retrieved-context models explain a broad range of episodic-memory phenomena through a changing context representation, bidirectional item-context associations, and competitive memory search [@howard2002distributed; @sederberg2008context; @polyn2009context].
Context reinstatement and item-context binding have also explained reminder-dependent learning effects previously attributed to reconsolidation: a reminder reinstates earlier context, and new material encoded in that state becomes retrievable from the earlier context [@hupbach2008dynamics; @sederberg2011human].
Applying context reinstatement, item-context binding, and competitive search to the trauma-film paradigm yields an account of both competitor formation and selective retrieval.

We propose that selective interference requires two conditions under retrieved-context theory.
First, a reminder must reinstate enough film-associated context, and the intervening task must form strong enough associations with that state, for task events to become consequential competitors during later film retrieval.
Second, deliberate recall must construct and maintain a cue that discriminates film candidates from those task competitors.
The proposal predicts reduced unguided recall with relatively preserved deliberate recall when both conditions hold.
Under those conditions, unguided recall depends strongly on shared contextual support, while deliberate recall also receives film-directed support that competitors do not receive.
The proposal also predicts relative preservation in recognition when the test supplies a candidate film item and bypasses context-guided candidate selection.

We test these predictions by implementing the two-condition proposal in an emotional Context Maintenance and Retrieval model [@polyn2009context; @talmi2019retrieved; @cohen2022memory].
The simulations follow a generalization-style modeling logic [@busemeyer2000model; @lohnas2023event].
Core parameters are anchored in an independent affective free-recall dataset [@dupertuys2026ukraine], and no trauma-film outcomes are fitted.
Simulation 1 varies reminder presence and effective task-context learning to test competitor formation.
Simulation 2 compares start-of-film context reinstatement, a maintained film-category cue, and retrieval monitoring to determine which control operations protect recall.
The recognition analysis tests how presenting a candidate film item for judgment changes where reminder-linked task competition enters retrieval.
Together, the simulations define a mechanistic alternative to selective-vulnerability accounts and identify conditions under which intrusive and voluntary remembering should appear more or less dissociated.

## Intentionality and Test Format in Selective Interference

Selective-interference studies are often described as comparing involuntary and deliberate memory, but the empirical contrast also depends on how each form of remembering is measured.
Diary measures count film memories after they inadvertently come to mind during daily life.
Laboratory intrusion tasks count film memories reported during a defined monitoring period, sometimes while film cues are present.
In both cases, participants report film memories when they occur without deliberately trying to recover film details.
Voluntary-memory tests differ in whether target film material must be recovered or is presented for judgment: free recall and specific-probe questions ask participants to bring film details to mind, whereas recognition asks participants to distinguish true from false film statements or film stills from lure images [@james2016trauma; @lau2019intrusive; @lau2021selectively].
Selective interference appears most consistent when intrusion reports are compared with recognition, and less uniform when film material must be brought to mind under more similar retrieval conditions.
@fig-empirical-examples illustrates variation in retrieval format across selected trauma-film studies [@james2015computer; @lau2019intrusive; @lau2021selectively; @mcconnell2026testing].

Comparisons between diary intrusion reports and recognition tests confound retrieval intentionality with retrieval format.
In immediate post-film Tetris studies, participants completed Tetris soon after film viewing and later reported fewer diary intrusions, while verbal or visual recognition remained similar across groups [@holmes2009can; @holmes2010key].
Delayed reminder-plus-Tetris studies used a later film reminder before Tetris and found a related pattern when diary or laboratory intrusion measures were paired with recognition [@james2015computer; @kessler2020visuospatial].
Later work pairing diary intrusions with recognition retained the same basic comparison [@asselbergs2024effectiveness].
In these studies, intrusion measures can count a film memory only after it comes to mind and is reported, whereas verbal and visual recognition tests present candidate film material for judgment [@lau2019intrusive; @lau2021selectively].
A reduction in intrusions with preserved recognition therefore does not, by itself, show that voluntary memory is preserved across retrieval formats.

Evidence is less consistent in designs that make intrusion and voluntary-memory measures more comparable.
Free recall and specific-probe questions make voluntary-memory performance depend on bringing film material to mind, matching a central requirement of intrusion reports [@lau2019intrusive].
Laboratory intrusion tasks collect reports during a defined period, making the setting more comparable to laboratory voluntary-memory tests than a week-long diary [@lau2019intrusive; @lau2021selectively].
Across matched recall and laboratory-report formats, effects of Tetris after a film reminder are less uniform.
Some designs still show reduced diary or laboratory intrusion reports with relatively preserved voluntary memory [@lau2019intrusive; @lau2021selectively].
A stricter matched-report design did not find the predicted reduction in involuntary memory [@mcconnell2026testing].

Variation across retrieval formats motivates a mechanistic account of when and why selective interference appears.
Recognition-based comparisons show selective interference more consistently.
The same comparisons confound retrieval intentionality with test format.
Attempts to compare recall-like measures across intentionality conditions are more methodologically robust, yet observe selective interference less consistently.
A complete account must therefore explain both how deliberate recall can remain preserved while unguided recall is reduced, as well as why selective interference depends on how retrieval is cued and measured.

# Conditions for Selective Interference in Retrieved-Context Theory

Retrieved-context theory treats selective interference as a problem of memory search under a cue that has lost diagnosticity.
The current context provides graded support to candidate items, and a retrieved or presented item reinstates context associated with its earlier occurrence [@howard2002distributed; @sederberg2008context; @polyn2009context].
When target and competitor events are associated with overlapping context, both can receive support during later search.
Whether interference appears selectively then depends on what additional information retrieval supplies for distinguishing target from competitor events.

The retrieved-context operations map directly onto the trauma-film sequence.
Film, delay, task, and filler periods are represented as event sequences through which context evolves.
A film reminder reinstates context associated with the earlier film before the task is encoded.
Task events learned in that reinstated state can later be supported alongside film events, and both enter the same context-guided candidate competition.
Unguided and deliberate retrieval can nevertheless differ in their starting context, the support applied during candidate selection, and the treatment of an off-target candidate after it has been sampled.

Two commitments carry the explanation.
<!-- FIXME: "the explanation" here is an underspecified pronoun! -->
Reminder-linked task events must acquire enough support from film-associated context to become consequential competitors, and deliberate retrieval must have a film-directed cue that those competitors do not share.
The competitor-learning condition explains why the reminder and the effective strength of task-context learning determine interference.
The discriminating-cue condition explains why some forms of deliberate retrieval can remain selective despite that interference.
Recognition provides a separate boundary condition because the test supplies an item to evaluate and bypasses context-guided candidate selection.

## Context-Guided Search and Source Organization

Retrieved-context models were developed to explain structured regularities in open-ended recall.
Free recall favors recently studied items, and successive recalls tend to come from nearby study positions [@kahana1996associative; @howard2002distributed; @sederberg2008context].
In these models, a gradually changing context state cues candidate items, and recalled items reinstate the contexts in which they were encoded.
Recency follows because the retrieval context remains similar to contexts from recent study and recall events.
Temporal contiguity follows because a recalled item reinstates context from its study position, which is similar to the contexts associated with nearby items.

Recall is also organized by shared content, task, and source.
Semantically related items, items encoded under the same task, and items from the same source can cluster during recall [@polyn2009context; @polyn2009task; @polyn2012neural; @morton2016predictive; @lohnas2023event].
CMR captures semantic and source organization by allowing each form of information to contribute to the context state that guides retrieval.
Semantic and source dimensions can make a retrieval cue more selective than temporal context alone: a target-category or source cue can favor one subset of items even while temporal associations continue to organize retrieval within that subset [@polyn2011semantic; @lohnas2026specialized].
Combining shared temporal support with selective non-temporal support is central to the retrieved-context explanation developed here.

Emotional memory gives source organization a further role in the model used here.
Emotional items can cluster together, and emotional material is often remembered better than neutral material [@talmi2004semantic; @talmi2007contribution; @talmi2013enhanced].
Emotional CMR represents affective information as a source-like context dimension and allows emotional items to form stronger source-context associations [@talmi2019retrieved; @cohen2022memory].
Film events therefore share an affective/source-context signal while remaining distinct items with different temporal associations.
Task and delay events remain available to the same sampling process and can acquire support from any temporal or source context active while they are encoded.
The affective/source-context representation and the maintained film-category cue are separate model constructs.
Neither construct formally implements the S-reps or C-reps in dual-representation theory.

## Reminder-Linked Competitor Encoding

Reminder-linked competitor learning occurs when a film reminder reinstates context from the earlier event before task events are encoded.
Presented or retrieved items recover associated context in retrieved-context models [@howard2002distributed; @sederberg2008context; @polyn2009context].
A film reminder therefore shifts the current state toward context from the film episode.
If task events are then learned while reinstated film context remains active, they acquire context-to-item associations that overlap with associations supporting film events.
Later film-oriented context can consequently support task candidates as well as film candidates.

General episodic-memory work already supports reminder-driven linking of new material to an earlier context.
When people are reminded of an earlier list before learning a new list, items from the new list later intrude into recall of the earlier list [@hupbach2008dynamics].
Sederberg et al. [-@sederberg2011human] reproduced the asymmetric intrusion pattern with established temporal-context operations: the reminder reinstated earlier-list context, and new items became associated with that reinstated state.
Their TCM account left the original-list associations intact.
The TCM simulation explained the intrusion by changing which items the earlier context could later retrieve.

Recall errors show why context-to-item associations with task events matter.
In multi-list free recall, people sometimes report items from earlier lists instead of the requested list, and those intrusions vary systematically with list recency and intervening context [@zaromb2006temporal; @howard2008persistence; @lohnas2015expanding].
Retrieved-context models explain such errors by allowing target and non-target items to enter the candidate set whenever both receive support from the current retrieval state.
Allowing all sufficiently supported items to enter the candidate set makes task and delay events eligible competitors in the trauma-film paradigm.
Task and delay candidates reduce film recall when they occupy sampling opportunities that would otherwise retrieve film events, even though the stored film-item associations remain in memory.

Competitor learning must also be strong enough to matter.
TCM, CMR, and eCMR have represented variation in encoding priority by scaling newly formed context-to-item associations, including effects attributed to rehearsal, focused attention, and preferential processing of emotional material [@sederberg2008context; @polyn2009context; @talmi2019retrieved].
The present model follows that formal precedent by varying effective task-context learning: how strongly task events become retrievable from the context active during the task.
Effective task-context learning is a formal model quantity.
Engagement is one possible psychological source of variation in that quantity.
The proposed link from engagement to task-context learning remains a hypothesis.

The available task comparisons reinforce that distinction.
Trauma-film participants report high compliance with and enjoyment of Tetris, consistent with sustained task engagement [@holmes2010key].
Yet active comparison tasks can be similarly engaging: Tetris and a quiz received comparable ratings of concentration, enjoyment, difficulty, and distraction, and word games as well as Tetris have sometimes reduced intrusions [@kessler2020visuospatial; @hagenaars2017tetris].
Substantial processing may help task events become consequential competitors.
Selective preservation additionally requires task events to remain distinguishable from film events by information available to a film-directed retrieval cue.

## Film-Directed Control Under Matched Recall Conditions

Better-matched retrieval designs sharpen the contrast between unguided and deliberate film retrieval because both conditions require film material to be brought to mind and reported.
Vigilance-intrusion tasks collect memories that arise during an ongoing task, sometimes in the presence of film cues, whereas voluntary versions can retain the same cues and reporting format while asking participants to search deliberately for film memories [@lau2019intrusive; @lau2021selectively; @mcconnell2026testing].
Once candidate-item presentation is held more nearly constant, the central difference is whether participants deliberately search for film memories.
The retrieved-context account explains where that control enters the retrieval cycle and which form of control can protect recall from task candidates already supported by film-associated context.

Deliberate retrieval can intervene at three stages.
It can reinstate target context before sampling begins, maintain a target-selective cue while candidates are sampled, or monitor a sampled candidate before that candidate shapes subsequent search.
Each operation changes a different stage of retrieval.
Changing the starting context affects which candidates initially receive support; a maintained film-category cue changes their relative support during selection; and monitoring changes what follows after an off-target candidate has already been sampled.
@fig-retrieved-context-retrieval-operations separates these three control points.

Start-of-film context reinstatement provides film-oriented support before the first retrieval attempt.
When people are asked to recall an earlier list after studying a more recent list, early responses can be biased toward the instructed list, and delayed free recall often begins near the start of the target list [@lohnas2015expanding; @healey2024peppr; @howard1999contextual; @healey2014memory; @herrema2024first].
Retrieved-context accounts explain target-list and start-of-list biases by evolving the current state toward context associated with the beginning of the target list before search begins [@kragel2015neural; @morton2016predictive; @healey2024peppr].
Start-of-film reinstatement initially favors early film events.
Its protection is limited, however, because ordinary sampling resumes from a context dimension that reminder-linked task learning has already made less selective.

Retrieval monitoring acts after a candidate has been sampled.
In externalized recall, participants report all words that come to mind and identify many intrusions as errors, showing that off-target candidates can enter retrieval without being accepted as target memories [@unsworth2010understanding; @lohnas2015expanding].
Sampled intrusions can nevertheless pull subsequent search toward their own temporal or semantic context [@zaromb2006temporal; @unsworth2010understanding].
Retrieved-context implementations therefore allow a rejected item to influence later context while varying the strength of that update [@lohnas2015expanding].
In the present account, monitoring dampens the context update from a sampled non-film item.
Monitoring can help search return to film material after an intrusion.
The initial competition has already occurred by the time monitoring evaluates the sampled task item.

A maintained film-category cue acts directly during candidate selection.
People can restrict recall to a target category while preserving temporal organization within the selected subset, and category-selective neural activity remains elevated between responses and weakens before extra-category intrusions [@polyn2011semantic; @norman2017neuronal; @lohnas2026specialized].
CMR already allows semantic, task, and source information to support candidates alongside temporal context [@polyn2009context; @polyn2009task; @morton2016predictive].
Selective-retrieval studies further show that target selection is strongest when external cues overlap more with target than competing traces, while internally maintained goals can also prepare or amplify target-relevant information [@moccia2022cue; @moccia2025effects].
Evidence from category-directed recall and selective retrieval motivates a maintained semantic or category cue that supports film events without equally supporting task events.

The diagnosticity of that cue is a separate condition from competitor strength.
Film and Tetris both contain visuospatial information, so modality cannot supply a perfectly distinguishing cue.
The proposed film-category cue distinguishes event categories along semantic, item-feature, task, or source dimensions that a film-directed goal can exploit.
The current implementation represents film-task cue discriminability in reduced form by adding support to items marked as film events.
The implementation therefore assumes that the cue discriminates film from task candidates and does not derive that discrimination from represented film and task content.

Competitor strength and cue diagnosticity yield three cases.
When task-context learning is weak, little interference should occur regardless of retrieval control.
When task-context learning is strong and the maintained film-category cue is diagnostic, unguided film recall can be reduced while deliberate recall remains relatively protected.
When task-context learning is strong but the film-directed cue also supports task candidates, deliberate and unguided recall should both be impaired.
Cue discriminability is fixed in the current model, so the simulations do not include the final case.
Impairment of both deliberate and unguided recall remains a necessary prediction when task competitors also match the film-directed cue.
